question:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.

Passage: When electric motors began to replace steam engines in American factories in the 1880s, productivity statistics barely moved, and they did not move appreciably for nearly four decades. Economic historians who have studied this lag reject the simple explanation that the new technology was inferior; electricity was cheaper and more flexible than steam from early on. The difficulty lay elsewhere. Factories had been designed around a central steam engine that drove a single shaft, with machines clustered close to it and multi-storey buildings that minimised the length of the belts. Owners who merely swapped the engine for an electric motor kept this layout and therefore captured only marginal savings. The real gains came when a later generation of managers realised that each machine could carry its own small motor, which freed them to build single-storey plants arranged around the flow of production rather than the location of power. This reorganisation, not the motor, raised output. The episode is now invoked to explain why recent investments in information technology were also slow to show up in national statistics. The analogy is suggestive but should not be pressed too far. Electrification required replacing physical capital, which firms do slowly because plants are long-lived, whereas software can be altered quickly. On the other hand, the complementary assets that digital technology demands - new skills, new forms of organisation, trust in data - are intangible, and intangibles are poorly captured by conventional accounting, so measured productivity may understate real gains for years. A sceptic may therefore argue that the paradox is partly an artefact of measurement. Yet this reading is incomplete too, for it cannot account for the fact that many firms which adopted the technology early gained nothing. What the history suggests is less that technology takes time to mature than that its benefits are conditional on the willingness of organisations to unlearn the arrangements built around the technology it replaces.

Q. Which one of the following best expresses the central argument of the passage?
options: (a) Electric motors were adopted slowly because they were initially costlier than steam engines.
(b) The benefits of a general-purpose technology depend on reorganising work around it, which is why measured productivity can lag adoption by decades.
(c) Productivity statistics are so unreliable that they cannot be used to judge technological progress.
(d) Information technology will inevitably reproduce the four-decade lag seen with electrification.
explanation: (b) The passage's closing sentence says benefits are conditional on organisations unlearning old arrangements; (a) is rejected in para 1, (c) overstates the measurement point, (d) is contradicted by the caution against pressing the analogy.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Main idea - organisational change and the productivity paradox

Q. Which one of the following can be most reasonably inferred from the passage?

(b) Software-based technologies take exactly as long as physical machinery to yield gains.
(c) A firm that installs advanced digital tools but retains its old workflows and reporting hierarchy is likely to realise only modest gains.

Q. The author's claim that benefits are 'conditional on the willingness of organisations to unlearn' rests on which one of the following assumptions?
options: (a) Early adopters that gained nothing differed from the successful ones in how they organised work, not in the quality of the technology they had access to.
(b) Intangible assets such as skills and trust can never be measured by any accounting method.
(c) Electrification and information technology are alike in every important respect.
(d) Managers of the 1880s were less competent than managers of today.

micro_topic: Assumption - why early adopters gained nothing

question:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.

Passage: We tend to speak of forgetting as a failure - a leak in the vessel of memory - and to measure the health of a mind by how much it retains. Yet a being that forgot nothing would not be a perfect thinker but an incapacitated one. Memory that preserves every detail of every experience offers no way to distinguish what matters from what merely happened; generalisation, which is the essence of thought, depends upon discarding particulars. The same holds for societies. Communities that remember every grievance with perfect fidelity cannot reconcile, and the durable peace that follows civil conflict has often rested on a tacit, collective agreement not to speak of certain things. It would be a mistake, however, to conclude that forgetting is simply to be welcomed. There is a difference between forgetting that occurs because experience has been absorbed and transformed, and forgetting that is manufactured by those who gain from silence. The first allows a past to recede; the second erases it. The victims of an atrocity who are told to move on are not being invited to forget but to forgo a claim, and the language of healing often disguises what is in truth a demand for convenience. What distinguishes the two cases is not how much is forgotten but who decides, and for whose benefit. A society that forgets by choice and with the participation of those who suffered has done something morally different from one whose forgetting has been engineered by its beneficiaries, even if the resulting silence is identical. The task, then, is neither to prize memory without limit nor to celebrate oblivion, but to ask of any forgetting whether it is something that has been done by people or merely done to them.

Q. The central point of the passage is that
options: (a) memory should be preserved as completely as possible in healthy minds and societies.
(b) forgetting is a necessary virtue and should be encouraged after every conflict.
(c) collective silence about the past is always evidence of oppression.
(d) the moral worth of forgetting depends on who decides and for whose benefit, not on how much is forgotten.
explanation: (d) Stated in the penultimate and final sentences. (a) and (b) are one-sided; (c) overgeneralises.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Main idea - forgetting, memory and legitimacy

Q. Which one of the following practices would the author most likely regard as morally objectionable?
options: (a) A village council, after hearing the victims, closes an old dispute with their free consent.
(b) A government declares a blanket amnesty and bans public discussion of past abuses, without consulting victims, citing 'national unity'.
(c) A student forgets minor details of a lecture while retaining its key principles.
(d) A community lets old grievances fade as new generations absorb the past into shared memory.
explanation: (b) It is forgetting engineered from above, 'done to' people. The others involve consent, ordinary cognition or organic absorption.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Inference - applying the argument to a new case

Q. The author's attitude towards appeals to victims to 'move on' is best described as
options: (c) wary scepticism toward its use as a cloak for convenience
explanation: (c) The author says such language 'often disguises a demand for convenience' yet still accepts consensual forgetting, so (b) is too extreme.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Tone and attitude - towards calls to 'move on'

question: Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G sit in a row, all facing north. G sits at one of the two ends. Exactly two persons sit between G and D. B sits third from the left end. F sits immediately to the left of E. A sits second to the left of E (that is, exactly one person sits between A and E). C does not sit next to D. Who sits exactly in the middle of the row?
explanation: Method: B is 3rd from left. G at an end and two persons between G and D gives (G,D) = (1,4) or (7,4) [or (4,...) not possible]. Try G=1,D=4: remaining places 2,5,6,7 for A,C,E,F. 'FE' adjacent with A two places left of E: F=6,E=7,A=5, so C=2, and C is not next to D (2 vs 4). Check G=7, D=4: places 1,2,5,6 remain; 'FE' must be (1,2) or (5,6), putting E at 2 or 6, so A would be at 0 or 4 - impossible. Order: G C B D A F E. Middle (4th) = D. Answer (d).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Linear arrangement - seven persons in a row

question: Five persons P, Q, R, S and T sit in a row, all facing north, and each drinks a different beverage - tea, coffee, milk, juice or water. R sits in the middle. Q sits to the right of R, and exactly one person sits between P and Q. Q drinks juice and P drinks coffee. The tea drinker sits next to the coffee drinker but not at either end. The milk drinker sits somewhere to the left of the juice drinker. The water drinker sits at one end. S sits to the right of T. Who drinks milk?
explanation: Method: R=3; Q to the right of R and one person between P and Q gives Q=4, P=2 (Q=5 would put P at 3). S, T take 1 and 5 with S right of T, so T=1, S=5. Tea is adjacent to coffee (P=2) and not at an end, so position 3: R drinks tea. Milk is left of juice (Q=4) and positions 2, 3 are taken, so milk is at 1: T. Water is then S at the end. Order T P R Q S = milk, coffee, tea, juice, water. Answer (a).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Row arrangement with attributes

question:
In the following question the symbols have these meanings: 'A @ B' means A is greater than B; 'A # B' means A is not greater than B; 'A $ B' means A is equal to B.

Statements: M @ N, N $ O, O @ P

Conclusions:
I. M @ P
II. P # N
III. O $ M

Which of the conclusions definitely follow?
explanation: Method: M > N = O > P. So M > P (I true). P < N so P is not greater than N (II true). O = N < M so O = M is false (III false). Answer (b).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Coded inequalities

question: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand of a clock at 7:20?
explanation: Method: Hour hand = 7 x 30 + 20 x 0.5 = 220°. Minute hand = 20 x 6 = 120°. Difference = 100°. Formula check: |30H - 5.5M| = |210 - 110| = 100°. Answer (c).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Clocks - angle between hands

question:
Statements:
All pens are books.
Some books are files.
No file is a register.

Conclusions:
I. Some books are not registers.
II. No pen is a register.
III. Some pens are files.
IV. Some files are books.

Which of the conclusions follow?
explanation: Method: Draw pens inside books; the 'files' circle overlaps books but is wholly outside registers. The books that are files are not registers, so I follows. IV is the simple conversion of 'Some books are files'. Pens may or may not touch files or registers, so II and III do not follow. Answer (b).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Syllogism - valid conclusions with conversion

question:
Study the table showing passenger traffic at four airports and answer the two questions that follow (Set 1).

| Airport | Passengers 2019 (lakh) | Passengers 2023 (lakh) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 80 | 96 |
| B | 25 | 40 |
| C | 60 | 66 |
| D | 30 | 36 |

Q. Which airport recorded the highest absolute increase in passengers, and which the highest percentage growth, between 2019 and 2023, respectively?
explanation: Method: Increases A 16, B 15, C 6, D 6, so A is highest in absolute terms. Growth: A 20%, B 60%, C 10%, D 20%, so B is highest in percentage. Trap: assuming the biggest gainer also grew fastest. Answer (c).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Table - absolute increase vs percentage growth (trap)

question:
Refer to the airport traffic table in the previous question (Set 1).

| Airport | Passengers 2019 (lakh) | Passengers 2023 (lakh) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 80 | 96 |
| B | 25 | 40 |
| C | 60 | 66 |
| D | 30 | 36 |

Q. What was the overall percentage growth in the combined traffic of the four airports between 2019 and 2023?
explanation: Method: 2019 total = 195, 2023 total = 238; growth = 43/195 = 22.05%. Trap: (20+60+10+20)/4 = 27.5% (simple average ignores weights); 43 is the absolute increase. Answer (b).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Table - aggregate growth vs average of percentages (trap)

question:
A company's budget was ₹600 crore in 2023 and ₹800 crore in 2024. The percentage allocated to each head is given below (Set 2).

| Head | 2023 share of ₹600 crore budget | 2024 share of ₹800 crore budget |
|---|---|---|
| R&D | 30% | 25% |
| Marketing | 25% | 20% |
| Operations | 35% | 45% |
| Administration | 10% | 10% |

Q. For how many heads did the rupee allocation rise from 2023 to 2024 even though the percentage share fell?
explanation: Method: Amounts 2023: 180, 150, 210, 60; 2024: 200, 160, 360, 80. R&D (30%->25%) rose 180->200; Marketing (25%->20%) rose 150->160. Operations' share rose; Administration's share was unchanged. So 2 heads. Answer (c).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Caselet - share vs absolute amount (trap)

question:
Refer to the budget data in the previous question (Set 2).

| Head | 2023 share of ₹600 crore budget | 2024 share of ₹800 crore budget |
|---|---|---|
| R&D | 30% | 25% |
| Marketing | 25% | 20% |
| Operations | 35% | 45% |
| Administration | 10% | 10% |

Q. Suppose the Operations allocation in 2025 is 20% higher than in 2024 and the total budget in 2025 is ₹1,000 crore. What percentage of the 2025 budget goes to Operations?
explanation: Method: Operations 2024 = 0.45 x 800 = 360 crore. 2025 = 360 x 1.2 = 432 crore. Share = 432/1000 = 43.2%. Trap: 45% x 1.2 = 54% ignores the larger base. Answer (b).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Caselet - projection from a share base (trap)

question: You are a Deputy Director. Your Director and a Joint Secretary from a sister wing have each given you verbal and conflicting instructions on which of two urgent tasks to complete first. Both tasks are due tomorrow. What would you do?
options: (a) Follow the officer who is higher in rank and say nothing to the other.
(b) Inform both officers of the conflict, request that they agree a priority (preferably in writing), and meanwhile progress the parts of both tasks that are common.
(c) Quietly do half of each task so that neither officer is displeased.
(d) Wait until the two officers resolve the matter between themselves before starting.
explanation: (b) Transparent, rule-abiding and keeps work moving; (a) conceals, (c) risks both tasks, (d) wastes time.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Conflicting instructions from two superiors

question: You head a pension office. Shortly before closing time an 82-year-old pensioner arrives without the documents needed for annual verification and cannot use the online life-certificate system. The rules require verification before payment. What would you do?
options: (a) Explain the position kindly, use the permitted assisted or alternative verification routes, help him complete the formalities, and fix a follow-up if anything is still pending.
(b) Ask him to return another day with all the documents.
(c) Release the pension without verification because of his age.
(d) Ask his relatives to come and do nothing for him now.
explanation: (a) Balances compassion with rules; (b) and (d) are rigid and unhelpful, (c) violates procedure.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Empathy within rules - elderly pensioner

question: You discover that a close friend and colleague has submitted a travel allowance claim that is clearly inflated. Nobody else has noticed. What would you do?
options: (a) Ignore it, as it is a small amount and he is your friend.
(b) Tell your colleagues so that they put pressure on him.
(c) Verify the facts, speak to him privately, advise him to correct the claim, and report to the competent authority through proper channels if he does not.
(d) Send an anonymous complaint to the media.
explanation: (c) Fair, verifies before acting, gives a chance to correct and escalates properly; (a) condones, (b) and (d) are improper.
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Integrity - a friend's inflated claim

question: Pipe A can fill a tank in 12 hours and pipe B in 18 hours, while pipe C can empty the full tank in 9 hours. A and B are opened together; after 6 hours C is also opened. In how many hours in total will the tank be full?
explanation: Method: Rates per hour: A 1/12, B 1/18, C -1/9. A+B = 5/36; in 6 h they fill 30/36 = 5/6. With C open, net = 5/36 - 4/36 = 1/36. Remaining 1/6 takes 6 h. Total = 12 h. Answer (b).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Pipes and cisterns - staged opening

question: What is the difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on ₹8,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum?
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Compound vs simple interest - 3 years

question: In how many distinct arrangements of the letters of the word BALLOON do the two L's NOT come together?
explanation: Method: Total = 7!/(2!2!) = 1260 (two L's and two O's repeat). With the two L's glued, treat as one letter: 6!/2! = 360. Not together = 1260 - 360 = 900. Answer (a).
subject: CSAT
micro_topic: Permutations with repeated letters
